name: Suction cup / cupping on cheeks

lead: Facial cupping uses small suction cups on the cheeks. Users hope it gives a fuller, more lifted and more colorful cheek area, and it is usually done in short sessions with light suction.
It is an offshoot of traditional body cupping, adapted for the face. Results people describe are temporary, and no published trials have tested it for cheek shaping.

paras: A cup creates a partial vacuum that pulls skin and underlying tissue upward into it. This briefly brings blood to the surface, which proponents link to a flushed, lifted look.

Suction can break tiny capillaries and leave circular marks or bruises, and strong suction on thin facial skin is where most reported marks come from. Cupping is generally regarded as suitable for most people when done by trained practitioners, but conditions such as eczema or psoriasis can be aggravated.

chain: Suction cup draws cheek skin into the cup
Temporary flush and lift in the area
angle.text: People use small suction cups on the cheeks hoping for a temporary lift, a flush of color and a more contoured look. The effect described by users is short-lived and tied to the suction session itself.

lead: Cupping on the cheeks is the use of small suction cups on the face, borrowed from the wider practice of cupping therapy, with the aim of giving the cheek area a fuller, livelier and more contoured look. A cup is applied to the skin and a partial vacuum draws the tissue gently upward into it; people who try it on the face do so for a temporary flush of color and a lifted appearance in the cheeks and lower face.[1]

In looksmaxxing and skincare circles the technique is discussed as a low-cost, at-home way to work on facial appearance. Proponents describe the suction as bringing blood to the surface of the skin, which they associate with a healthier-looking complexion and a lifted look. Cupping on the body has been used in many traditions, from Chinese and Middle Eastern medicine to ancient Greece, and the face version is an adaptation of it, typically with small, softer cups and lighter suction than those used on the back.[1]

Cupping in general leaves circular marks where small capillaries beneath the skin respond to the suction. A 2020 eye-tracking study of cupping marks found that people notice and attend to these marks, which is one reason facial cupping is often described as done with light suction and short sessions.[2] No published trials have tested cheek cupping for cosmetic results.

paras: Cups used on the face are typically small silicone or plastic cups that are squeezed or pumped to create suction, in contrast to the larger glass or bamboo cups used on the back. Cupping therapy more broadly includes dry cupping (suction only), fire cupping, and wet cupping, and cups may be left in place or glided over oiled skin as a cup massage.[1]

Cupping sessions in traditional settings usually last between five and fifteen minutes per placement, and suction strength is classed as light, medium or strong.[1] Facial applications are generally described at the light end of that range.

Facial cupping is discussed as a do-it-yourself approach to cheek definition and skin glow, alongside other manual face techniques such as massage and gua sha. Users describe moving the cup across the cheek or holding it briefly in place. Because the marks cupping can leave are visible, users commonly describe keeping suction light on the face.[2]

Facial gua sha, a related scraping practice, became popular with beauty influencers on social media around 2021 to 2022, for claimed lymphatic drainage and skin freshening; cupping on the face is often presented in the same circles.[3]

Suction breaks small capillaries under the skin, which produces circular bruises or petechiae. Other reported risks of cupping include burns with fire cupping, skin discoloration, and flare-ups of eczema or psoriasis.[1] The U.S. National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health is cited as noting persistent discoloration, scars and infections as possible side effects.[1] Research on how people react to cupping marks shows they draw visual attention, which is relevant on the face.[2]

No studies found on cupping the cheeks. Studies of cupping therapy on the body have examined mainly pain conditions, and a 2025 randomized trial looked at its immediate effects on pain, flexibility and temperature of the lower back.[4] Reviews describe the wider cupping literature as variable in quality.[1]
